I'm Abhinav, and last summer my friend Mohit and I ran a weekend dosa stall at the Koramangala flea market. After the last Sunday, sitting in an auto with a crate of unused batter, I said, "That was a complete disaster. We should never have tried."

Mohit said, "Rate it. One to ten."

I wanted to say one. But then I actually thought. We sold out on two Saturdays. People came back for the podi dosa. Our tawa was too small, we never worked out the queue, and the rain on the last weekend killed us.

I said, "Maybe five?"

He said, "Then write the five good things and the five bad ones." We did it on the back of the menu card. On paper, it wasn't a disaster. It was a first try. This year we're back, with two tawas.

Supervisor's note, water project, Latur, 4 November.

After Friday's review, Jagdish told me the rainwater tank pilot was "a total failure" and asked to be taken off it. He was pale and had clearly not slept.

I asked him to rate the pilot from one to ten instead of pass or fail. He said two. Then I asked him to list, in two columns, what worked and what didn't. Worked: eleven of fifteen tanks built on time; the village committee now meets weekly; the women's group keeps the logbook. Didn't: four tanks leak at the joints, and the pipe order came late.

By the end he said, "Maybe six." We agreed he stays on the project, with one job this month: find out why the joints leak.

I'll check in with him on Wednesday.

Nirmala

School counsellor's note, 18 January.

Ritu came to my room at lunch, tearful. Her best friend, Pooja, hadn't replied to her messages since Sunday night. Ritu had already decided what it meant: Pooja was angry, had told the whole class something, and "nobody will sit with me ever again". She said each step as if it had already happened.

I asked her to write down what she actually knew. It was short: Pooja hasn't replied since Sunday; Pooja was absent today. Then I asked what else could explain those two facts. She came up with: Pooja is sick, her phone is broken, a family trip.

With Ritu's permission, I checked with the office: Pooja's mother had called in; Pooja has a fever.

Ritu laughed and cried at the same time. We agreed she'll send one kind message: "Heard you're sick, feel better." I'll check in with Ritu on Friday.

Jatin

Akash, you think your teacher hates you because you're not in the play? Listen to your Gargi Dadi. When I was ten, in Allahabad, Sister Agnes chose girls for the Christmas play. I wasn't chosen at all. Not even as a shepherd.

I went home and cried. "Sister Agnes thinks I'm stupid. She never liked me. She looks at me like I'm a nuisance." I believed every word as if she had said it.

My mother asked, "Did she say that?" I said, "No, but I know."

The next week Sister Agnes called me to her room. She wanted me to read the story aloud from the side of the stage, because I read the most clearly in the class. The narrator! The most words of anyone.

I had spent a whole week sure of her thoughts. I was wrong about every single one.

qa.q: Who chose the girls for the Christmas play?
qa.a: Sister Agnes chose them.

qa.q: Why did young Gargi believe Sister Agnes thought she was stupid?
qa.a: Young Gargi felt rejected and hurt at not being chosen, and treated her own guesses about the teacher as if they had been said aloud.

qa.q: What question in the story could have saved Gargi a week of pain?
qa.a: Her mother's "Did she say that?" pointed to checking; asking Sister Agnes directly would have revealed the narrator role sooner.

qa.q: What was Sister Agnes actually thinking about Gargi?
qa.a: Sister Agnes thought Gargi read the most clearly in the class and wanted her as the narrator.

grounding: A grandmother recalls being sure, as a girl left out of a play, that her teacher thought her stupid, and being wrong.

passage:
It was the week the family was shifting flats, everything in cardboard boxes, and Disha had no time to practise. On Tuesday Sangeeta ma'am put up the list for the annual day dance. Disha's name wasn't on it.

She read it twice, then walked out stiffly. On the bus home she decided: Sangeeta ma'am thinks I'm clumsy. She saw me trip in PT. She thinks I'll ruin the dance. She probably laughs about me in the staff room.

At home she sat on a box and wouldn't unpack. "Ma'am hates me," she told her father, who was taping up kitchen boxes.
"Did she say so?"
"No. But it's obvious."
"Is it? Or is it just the story you're telling?"
Disha scowled. The next day, still grumpy, she asked Sangeeta ma'am. "You were absent for the auditions, Disha," ma'am said. "The shift, remember? There's a second group next week."

qa.q: Why was Disha's name not on the list?
qa.a: Disha was absent for the auditions because of the shift.

qa.q: Why did Disha feel so sure Sangeeta ma'am thought she was clumsy?
qa.a: Disha felt hurt and embarrassed, and in a stressful week her worry about tripping in PT turned into "facts" about her teacher's thoughts.

qa.q: Which choice turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Asking Sangeeta ma'am directly, even while grumpy, replaced the imagined story with the real reason and a second chance.

qa.q: How might Disha's father see the situation while taping boxes?
qa.a: Disha's father seems calm and gently doubtful, asking whether it is fact or just the story she is telling.

grounding: During a house move a girl left off the dance list decides her teacher thinks she is clumsy, until she asks.

passage:
The rain had soaked Rajni's uniform on the way, so she was wearing her cousin's old one: faded, too long in the sleeves, the school crest half peeled off. She'd rolled the sleeves three times.

In the second period she saw Tanvir lean over to Mehul and whisper something. Mehul glanced her way and grinned.

That was it. She knew exactly what they'd said: look at Rajni's uniform, she looks like she's wearing a sack. The words felt as real as if she'd heard them. She spent chemistry with her arms folded tightly over the crest. At lunch she sat in the library instead of the canteen.

When the last bell rang, Tanvir came up to her desk. "Rajni, Mehul and I were saying you should be quiz captain. You got every answer in second period. Will you?"

Rajni stared at him, arms still folded.

qa.q: Why was Rajni wearing her cousin's old uniform?
qa.a: The rain had soaked her own uniform on the way.

qa.q: Why was Rajni so sure Tanvir and Mehul were mocking her?
qa.a: Rajni felt self-conscious and embarrassed about the faded uniform, so her own worry became the words she imagined them saying.

qa.q: What could Rajni try next time she sees whispering?
qa.a: Rajni could remind herself she doesn't know what was said, or simply ask, before hiding in the library.

qa.q: What were Tanvir and Mehul actually talking about?
qa.a: They were saying Rajni should be quiz captain because she got every answer in second period.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl in a borrowed uniform who is certain two whispering classmates are mocking her clothes.

passage:
Vinita had begged for the pink sneakers for weeks, and on Monday she wore them to her Chandigarh school for the first time. At assembly she noticed Gurleen and Harleen looking at her feet and whispering behind their hands.

Her ears went hot. Obviously they were saying: those shoes are so childish, pink, like a baby's. She could almost hear Gurleen's laugh.

By break she'd taken them off and put on her old PT shoes from her locker. She didn't talk to anyone. When Gurleen waved at her in the corridor, Vinita looked away.

At home that evening, a message from Gurleen: "omg where did you get those pink shoes?? me and Harleen want the same 😍 pls tell"

Vinita looked at the message for a long time. Then at the pink shoes in her bag.

qa.q: Where did Vinita keep her old PT shoes?
qa.a: Vinita kept them in her locker.

qa.q: Why did Vinita feel sure the whispering was about her shoes being childish?
qa.a: Vinita was anxious about the new pink shoes, so she treated her imagined version of their thoughts as words they had spoken.

qa.q: What might have helped Vinita at assembly?
qa.a: Vinita could have noticed she didn't know what they said, or asked them, instead of hiding the shoes and ignoring Gurleen.

qa.q: What were Gurleen and Harleen actually thinking?
qa.a: They admired the shoes and wanted the same ones.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl sure that two whispering classmates are mocking her new shoes, when they actually admire them.

passage:
"Did you see them?" Afreen hissed, pulling Zainab behind the notice board.
"Who?"
"Nazneen and Priti. By the water cooler. They looked at my kurta and laughed."
"I saw them laughing. I didn't see them looking at your kurta."
"They obviously were. It's Ammi's old one. The colour's so dull. They think I look like somebody's aunty."
"Did they say that?"
"They didn't have to."
Zainab raised her eyebrows. "Afreen, Nazneen was showing Priti a video on her phone. The one with the goat on the school bus."
"...What goat?"
"Everyone's been watching it all morning. You're the only one who hasn't."
Afreen let go of her dupatta. "Oh."
"Also," Zainab said, "your kurta's nice. Your Ammi has good taste."

qa.q: What was Nazneen actually showing Priti?
qa.a: Nazneen was showing Priti a video on her phone, the one with the goat on the school bus.

qa.q: Why was Afreen sure they were laughing at her kurta?
qa.a: Afreen felt self-conscious about wearing Ammi's old kurta, so she took her own worry as their thoughts.

qa.q: What did Zainab do that helped Afreen check the story?
qa.a: Zainab separated what she saw from what Afreen assumed, asked "Did they say that?", and shared the real reason for the laughing.

qa.q: What were Nazneen and Priti actually laughing about?
qa.a: They were laughing at the goat video everyone had been watching all morning.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl certain that laughing classmates are mocking her kurta, until a friend checks the story.

passage:
Dear Shalini,

I didn't get to say this properly at dinner, so I'm writing it.

When we were planning the Goa trip and I went quiet, you said, "You clearly hate the plan. Just say it." I understand why it looked like that. I wasn't talking; I was staring at my plate.

But honestly, I wasn't angry at all. I'd had two lab reports due that day and had slept four hours. I was just tired. When you said I hated it, I felt misread, then a bit hurt, and then I didn't know how to explain without sounding defensive.

So here it is: I love the plan. I'm excited about the beach day and the fort. Next time I go quiet, could you ask, "Are you okay?" instead? I'll try to say "I'm tired" out loud.

See you Friday,
Urmila

qa.q: How many hours had Urmila slept?
qa.a: Urmila had slept four hours.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel when Shalini said "You clearly hate the plan"?
qa.a: Urmila felt misread and a bit hurt, since the quiet came from tiredness, not anger.

qa.q: What does Urmila suggest for next time, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Shalini could ask "Are you okay?" and Urmila could say "I'm tired" aloud, so guesses are replaced by checking.

qa.q: Why might Shalini have read Urmila's silence as anger?
qa.a: Shalini saw Urmila staring at the plate and not talking, and without asking, filled the silence with a guess.

grounding: A letter from a tired, quiet friend who was told they hated the trip plan, gently explaining what they actually felt.

passage:
Devika, can I just explain about last night? I'm Wasim, and I know you think I was angry about the film plan. You said, "You obviously hate it, you've got that face." Then you changed the whole plan to the café, and everyone went along.

But I wasn't angry. I'd done a double shift at the call centre and my head was buzzing. I wasn't thinking about the film at all; I was thinking about sleep.

When you said I hated it, I felt kind of trapped, like whatever I said next would sound angry. So I just shrugged, which probably made it worse.

So, honestly: I'm happy with the film or the café. I was just tired. If I look like that again, you can ask me. I'd much rather you ask than guess.

qa.q: Where had Wasim worked a double shift?
qa.a: Wasim had done a double shift at the call centre.

qa.q: What did Wasim feel when Devika said "You obviously hate it"?
qa.a: Wasim felt misread and a bit trapped, as though anything said next would sound angry.

qa.q: What does Wasim do now that could prevent the next misreading?
qa.a: Wasim explains the tiredness plainly and invites Devika to ask instead of guessing next time.

qa.q: Why might Devika have changed the whole plan?
qa.a: Devika probably read Wasim's face as anger and wanted to avoid a problem, not realising it was only tiredness.

grounding: Spoken to a friend, a tired young adult explains being wrongly read as angry about a plan and asks to be asked, not guessed.

passage:
Before, Monday: after a night shift at her part-time job, Dilnaz sat in the project meeting with her chin on her hand, saying little. Karthik looked at her and said, "Okay, Dilnaz clearly hates this plan. We'll change it." Everyone looked at her. Her face went hot. "No, I..." But they had already moved on.

During, Wednesday: in the corridor Karthik said, "You're still angry about Monday, na?" By now Dilnaz was a little annoyed, but not about the plan. About being told what she felt.

After, Friday: before the next meeting, she stopped him. "Karthik, on Monday I wasn't angry. I'd worked all night and was exhausted. The plan was fine. It just stung to be told I hated it." Karthik blinked. "Oh. I just assumed. Sorry."
"Next time, just ask," she said, smiling.

qa.q: What had Dilnaz done before Monday's meeting?
qa.a: Dilnaz had worked a night shift at her part-time job.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling by Wednesday?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt a little annoyed, not about the plan but about being told what she felt.

qa.q: Which choice on Friday worked, and why?
qa.a: Dilnaz calmly explained she was exhausted, not angry, and that being misread stung, so Karthik could apologise and learn to ask.

qa.q: Why might Karthik have assumed Dilnaz hated the plan?
qa.a: Karthik saw her quiet, chin on hand, and guessed anger without checking.

grounding: Over a week a tired student is told she hates a project plan, feels misread, and gently explains what she actually felt.

passage:
At the primary school in a village near Bijapur, Yusuf had been sure since morning that Sangeeta was annoyed with him. She hadn't returned his "namaste" at the gate. She'd walked past his classroom without looking in. At lunch she sat at the far end of the verandah.

By two o'clock Yusuf had built a whole case in his head. It must be the mid-day meal register he'd filled in late on Monday. She'd complain to the block officer. She'd say, "Yusuf sir is careless," in the next meeting.

At three, instead of stewing through the last period, he walked over. "Sangeeta ma'am, is something wrong? Did I upset you?"

She looked up, surprised, a hand pressed to her cheek. "Upset? No, Yusuf sir. I've had a toothache since last night. I can barely see straight."

Yusuf laughed at himself all the way home.

qa.q: Why had Sangeeta walked past without looking in?
qa.a: Sangeeta had a toothache since the night before and could barely see straight.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling by two o'clock?
qa.a: Yusuf felt anxious and uneasy, sure Sangeeta was annoyed and building a whole story about complaints.

qa.q: What did Yusuf's short question replace?
qa.a: It replaced hours of imagined complaints and meetings with the simple truth: a toothache.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta's day actually like?
qa.a: Sangeeta was in pain from a toothache, too distracted to notice greetings, with no idea Yusuf was worried.

grounding: Shows a village teacher sure a colleague is annoyed who finally asks directly and finds the real, unrelated reason.

passage:
In the Stockholm office, Ingrid presented her new schedule for the team, and Alejandro, who usually had a joke for everything, said only, "Fine," and looked at his laptop.

All afternoon Ingrid replayed it. He thinks it's a bad plan. He thinks I'm bossy because I'm new. He'll tell the others it won't work. By four o'clock she had drafted, in her head, a whole argument defending the schedule.

Then she remembered what her old manager used to say: "Check the story before you believe it."

She walked to his desk. "Alejandro, quick question. When I showed the schedule, you seemed quiet. Is something about it a problem? I'd rather hear it than guess."

He looked up, surprised. "The schedule? No, it's good. My daughter's sick at home. I've been checking my phone all day."

"Oh, I'm sorry. Go home if you need to."

He smiled. "Thanks. And thanks for asking."

qa.q: What did Alejandro say about the schedule?
qa.a: Alejandro said only, "Fine."

qa.q: What was Ingrid feeling as she replayed his "Fine"?
qa.a: Ingrid felt anxious and defensive, sure he thought she was bossy and the plan was bad.

qa.q: Why was Ingrid's question a good move?
qa.a: A quick, direct question replaced an afternoon of imagined arguments with the real reason and let her offer support.

qa.q: What was Alejandro's afternoon actually like?
qa.a: Alejandro was worried about his sick daughter and checking his phone all day, not thinking about the schedule.

grounding: Shows a new team lead sure a colleague dislikes her plan who checks the story with a direct question.
